title: NLP Foundations
audience: Someone comfortable writing Python who wants to understand modern NLP from tokens upwards, rather than by calling an API and hoping.
outcome_statement: You can explain how text becomes tokens, becomes vectors, becomes predictions — and you can read a transformer paper without it being a wall of notation.

prerequisites.description: Basic Python. No linear algebra needed to start, though module three is easier if you have met vectors and matrices before.

estimate_assumptions: Assumes prior Python, around five focused hours a week, and that you actually do the checkpoints. Individual pace varies enormously — treat this as a range, not a schedule.

modules.title: From text to tokens
modules.summary: How raw text becomes the discrete units a model consumes, and why that choice shapes everything downstream.

items.note: Start here rather than with embeddings. The vocabulary story explains a great deal of later model behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary.
A working pipeline you can run today, and a reminder that plenty of production NLP never touches a transformer.

checkpoint.title: Tokenise the same paragraph three ways
checkpoint.prompt: Take one paragraph of your own text. Tokenise it with simple whitespace splitting, with a subword tokenizer, and with spaCy. Compare the token counts, and see what each does with a made-up word like “flurbulent”.
checkpoint.how_to_self_assess: You can say in one sentence each why the counts differ, and which approach handles an unseen word best and why.

modules.title: Representations and embeddings
modules.summary: Turning tokens into vectors where geometric closeness means something, which is the substrate under search, clustering and retrieval.

items.note: Community-created, and the clearest available intuition for why vector similarity corresponds to meaning.
The practical toolkit. Read enough to build a small semantic search over your own documents.

checkpoint.title: Build a tiny semantic search
checkpoint.prompt: Embed twenty short documents of your own choosing, then retrieve the nearest three for a handful of queries. Include at least one query whose best answer shares no words with the document.
checkpoint.how_to_self_assess: The no-shared-words query returns something sensible, and you can explain why keyword search would have failed it.

modules.title: Attention and transformers
modules.summary: The architecture underneath nearly everything current, approached through intuition first and the original paper second.

items.note: Read this before the paper. Going the other way round is possible but considerably more painful.
The primary source. Short, and far more readable once the illustrated version has given you the shapes.
Optional. Worth it if you want to understand where the pretrain-then-fine-tune pattern came from.

modules.title: Building and evaluating something
modules.summary: Putting it together on a real task, and being honest about whether it worked.

items.note: Work through to fine-tuning. Written by the library's maintainers, so it reflects that ecosystem's conventions rather than a neutral survey.
Reference rather than reading. The generation parameters in particular explain a lot of otherwise baffling output.
Optional. Take this if you would rather build pipelines than fine-tune models.
Optional and substantial. The standard reference to keep beside you rather than to read through.
Optional. The depth option, with assignments that make you implement the ideas rather than call them.

completion_criteria: Every required item in all four modules marked complete, including both checkpoints.
